lines.text: אבה 5 אבי
and Vulg. render præsepe, i. e. crib,
manger, which both here and in Job
l. c. is not less apt and probable. Comp.
Arab. اَرِى, Chald. אוּרְיָא, stall and crib.
So אבוס is also used in the Talmud.
* אָבַח a root of doubtful signif. perh.
i. q. אָבַךְ, הָפַךְ, to turn, to turn about.
Hence
אִבְחָה f. once, Ez. 21, 20 אִבְחַת חֶרֶב
a turning of the sword, i. e. a sword
turning itself, perh. glittering, i. q. חֶרֶב
מִתְהַפֶּכֶת Gen. 3, 24. But more proba-
bly it should here read: טִבְחַת חֶרֶב the
slaughter of the sword; and this con-
jecture is supported by the Sept. σφάγια
ῥομφαίας, Chald. קְטִלֵי חַרְבָּא, and the
words of the text which follow, ah! it is
made bright, it is sharpened for slaugh-
ter, לְטֶבַח; comp. v. 14. 15. The Greek
words σφάγιον, σφαγή, are elsewhere
often put for the Heb. טֶבַח, טִבְחָה, טָבֹחַ.
אֲבַטִּיחִים (r. בָּטַח, by transp. for
טָבַח, طَبَخَ to cook) m. plur. melons,
Num. 11, 5. Corresponding is Arab.
بِطِّيخ by transp. for طِبِّيخ from طبخ
to cook, to ripen; like Gr. πέπων melon,
squash, from πέπτω, comp. בָּשַׁל. The
Hebrews prefixed the prosthetic א.—
From the above Arabic word comes the
Spanish budiecas, French pastêques.
אֲבִי pr. n. f. Abi, the mother of Heze-
kiah, 2 K. 18, 2. In the parallel passage
2 Chr. 29, 1, she is called more fully and
correctly אֲבִיָּה, which is also read in
some copies in 2 K. l. c.
אֲבִי־עַלְבוֹן (father of strength, i. e.
strong, from r. غلب prævaluit) Abi-
albon, pr. n. of one of David’s officers,
2 Sam. 23, 31; called also אֲבִיאֵל 1 Chr.
אֲבִיאֵל (father of strength, i. e.
strong) Abiel, pr. n. m. a) 1 Chr. 11, 32,
see אֲבִי־עַלְבוֹן. b) The grandfather of
king Saul, 1 Sam. 9, 1. 14, 51. In the
genealogical table in 1 Chr. 8, 33. 9, 39,
Ner is said to have been the grandfather
of Saul; but according to 2 Sam. 14, 5,
he was his uncle. The true descent was
as follows:
Abiel
Kish Ner
Saul Abner.
אֲבִיאָסָף (father of gathering, i. e.
gatherer,) Abiasaph, pr. n. of a Levite
of the family of Korah, Ex. 6, 24; called
also אֶבְיָסָף 1 Chr. 6, 8. 22. 9, 19.
אָבִיב m. (r. אָבַב) an ear of grain, a
green ear, Lev. 2, 14. Ex. 9, 31 הַשְּׂעוֹרָה
(בָּ)אָבִיב the barley was in the ear;
comp. for the syntax Cant. 2, 13. חֹדֶשׁ
הָאָבִיב the month Abib, i. e. of green
ears, afterwards called נִיסָן Nisan, be-
ginning with the new moon of April, or,
according to the Rabbins, of March;
the first month of the Heb. year, Ex.
אֲבִיגַיִל (whose father is exultation)
Abigail, pr. n. f. a) The wife of Nabal
and afterwards of David, 1 Sam. 25, 3. 14;
called also by contr. אֲבִיגַל v. 32. 2 Sam.
3, 3 Cheth. Comp. Arab. أَشْ for أَيْشْ
what? b) A sister of David, 1 Chr. 2,
16; called also אֲבִיגַל 2 Sam. 17, 25.
אֲבִידָן (father of the judge) Abidan,
pr. n. of a phylarch or chief of the tribe
of Benjamin in the time of the exodus,
אֲבִידָע (father of knowledge, i. e.
knowing, wise) Abidah, pr. n. of a son of
Midian, Gen. 25, 4.
אֲבִיָּה (i. q. אֲבִיָּהוּ whose father is
Jehovah) pr. n. Abijah.
1. Masc. a) The second son of Sam-
uel, 1 Sam. 8, 2. b) 1 Chr. 7, 8. c)
e) i. q. אֲבִיָּהוּ king of Judah, see the
next article.
2. Fem. a) 1 Chr. 2, 24. b) See in
אֲבִי.
אֲבִיָּהוּ (whose father is Jehovah)
also אֲבִיָּה (id.) pr. n. Abijah, king of
Judah, son and successor of Rehoboam,
2 Chr. 13, 1 sq. In the books of Kings
always written אֲבִיָּם Abijam, 1 K. 14,
31. 15, 1. 7. 8, i. e. father of the sea, vir
maritimus.

line_status.note: The Arabic carries only a fatha over the alif and a kasra under the ra; nothing is printed over the final ya — neither the shadda of B nor the shadda+tanwin of A — and no hamza is visible on the alif. Final ya is printed dotless (ى). Chaldee אוּרְיָא and the English match both readings.
The vowel under ṭet in קְטִלֵי is a single dot printed below the letter (hireq); there is no holem dot above the ṭet, so Reading A's קְטֹלֵי is wrong.

The first Hebrew item has segol under tet (three dots visible) and the third item has a holem dot above the bet with qamets under tet and furtive patach — i.e. טָבֹחַ, matching Reading A; Reading B's טָבַח/טֶבַח order is not what is printed.
The Arabic طبخ is printed with fatḥa strokes over the letters (clearly visible over ط and ب); Reading A omits the vowel points, Reading B matches the print.
The second Arabic word shows two kasras beneath (under ṭā and bā) and a shadda over the bā, i.e. طِبِّيخ, not طَبِيخ; the final root طبخ is printed bare with no fatḥas.
A separate vav letter with holem (וֹ) is clearly printed between ayin and resh — plene spelling, matching Reading A; Reading B's defective holem on ayin is wrong.

The vowel under the parenthesised bet is a qamets (horizontal bar with a short vertical tail), not the two vertical dots of a shewa; the bet also carries a dagesh. Qamets is also what the grammar requires (בְּ + הָ contracting to בָּ, "in the ear" with article).
